title: Dual-Branch HNSW Approach with Skip Bridges and LID-Driven Optimization

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to address two specific issues in HNSW-based approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search: (1) mitigating local optima and cluster disconnection during greedy search, and (2) improving graph construction speed. These objectives are not explicitly addressed in any prior paper. While [7] introduces HNSW and discusses its hierarchical structure, it does not focus on the specific problems of local optima or cluster disconnection. Similarly, [10] addresses performance degradation and unreachable points in real-time updates but does not target the same issues. No prior paper explicitly identifies or solves the dual objectives of this contribution.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves introducing a dual-branch HNSW graph structure to increase the diversity of navigation paths, allowing traversal from multiple directions. [11] discusses diverse k-NN graphs, which aim to improve search diversity, but it does not propose a dual-branch structure or explicitly address HNSW. [19] and [13] explore diverse paths in other contexts (e.g., robotic motion planning, navigation), but these are not directly tied to HNSW or ANN search. No prior paper proposes a substantively equivalent mechanism of dual-branch graph structures for ANN search.

### Evaluation
The evaluation involves testing on six CV/NLP datasets, measuring recall improvements (up to 30% for CV, 18% for NLP) and construction time reductions (up to 20%), with ablation studies showing the relative contribution of the dual-branch mechanism. This evaluation design — using recall as the primary metric and conducting ablation studies — is standard in ANN research. For example, [7], [3], and [8] all use recall as a metric and perform ablation studies to validate their methods. While the specific datasets and results differ, the evaluation design itself is covered by prior work.

### Domain
The domain is approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search and vector indexing. This is a well-established area addressed by numerous prior papers, including [7], [3], [8], and [10]. While this contribution targets specific issues within HNSW-based ANN search, it does not introduce a new application area.

This is a specific instance of the general problem of escaping local optima in iterative search. This is the standard evaluation protocol for new ANN graph-based indexing methods.
